Arrangement P — Row 1: column 1; Row 2: columns 1 to 4; Row 3: column 2. Arrangement Q — Row 1: column 1; Row 2: column 1; Row 3: columns 1 to 2; Row 4: column 2; Row 5: column 2. Arrangement R — Row 1: column 1; Row 2: column 1; Row 3: column 1; Row 4: columns 1 to 2; Row 5: column 1. Arrangement S — Row 1: column 3; Row 2: columns 1 to 4; Row 3: column 4. Which arrangement can NOT be folded into a cube?
questions.explanation: Fold by rolling a cube over the squares: in the odd one out two squares land on the same face or around the same corner, so it cannot close up. Rule of thumb: a 2 × 2 block of squares, or five squares in a row, never folds into a cube; a row of four with one square above and one below (any positions) always does.
questions.shortcut: Look for a 2×2 block or 5 in a row: those fail.

questions.questionText: A net of six squares carries the numbers 1 to 6, one on each square. Row 1: column 4 = 1; Row 2: column 1 = 5, column 2 = 6, column 3 = 3, column 4 = 2; Row 3: column 2 = 4. The net is folded into a cube. What is the sum of the numbers on the four faces that touch the face showing 4?
questions.explanation: Opposite pairs: 1–4, 2–6, 3–5. Face 4 is opposite 1, so its four neighbours sum to 21 − 4 − 1 = 16.
questions.shortcut: Neighbours total = 21 − face − its opposite.

questions.questionText: How many different nets (flat patterns, counting rotations and reflections as the same) can be folded into a cube?
questions.explanation: Listing all arrangements of six squares and testing each by folding, exactly 11 distinct patterns work.
questions.shortcut: Remember: 11 nets of a cube.

questions.questionText: How many squares does the net of a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has 6 faces, each represented by one square.

questions.questionText: A net of a cube is cut out from paper as one piece. How many of the cube's 12 edges remain joined as folds in the net?
questions.explanation: Six squares joined into one piece need 5 shared edges (a tree on 6 pieces). So 5 edges are folds and 7 are cut.
questions.shortcut: Folds = squares − 1 = 5.

questions.questionText: A cube is cut along some edges and flattened into a net. How many of its 12 edges are cut?
questions.explanation: The net keeps 5 edges as folds (6 squares joined in one piece), so 12 − 5 = 7 edges are cut.
questions.shortcut: Cut edges = 12 − 5.

questions.questionText: When a cube net is flattened, the boundary of the shape consists of how many unit edges?
questions.explanation: Six squares have 24 edges counted separately; the 5 shared edges are each counted twice, so boundary = 24 − 2×5 = 14.

questions.questionText: When a net is folded into a cube, the boundary edges of the net get glued in pairs. How many pairs are glued?
questions.explanation: The boundary has 14 unit edges (24 − 2×5). They join in pairs to form the 7 edges that were cut, so 7 pairs.

questions.questionText: Of the 11 distinct nets of a cube, how many contain a straight row of four squares?
questions.explanation: Four squares in a row with one square attached above and one below gives the (1,4,1) family. Testing each placement of the two squares up to symmetry gives 6 distinct nets.
questions.shortcut: The 1-4-1 family has 6 nets.

questions.questionText: What is the greatest number of squares that can lie in a single straight row of a cube net?
questions.explanation: Five or six in a row would wrap around the cube and overlap: four squares around the cube are the maximum.
questions.shortcut: Four squares wrap round the cube exactly once.

questions.questionText: In a cube net, three squares lie in a straight line. When folded, how are the first and third squares related?
options: They share a corner but not an edge
questions.explanation: Two squares in a line with exactly one square between them fold to opposite faces of the cube.
questions.shortcut: One square between = opposite.

questions.questionText: In a net of a cube, a straight row of four squares is folded. When closed, how do the first and fourth squares of that row relate?
options: They are adjacent faces sharing an edge
They are not touching at all
questions.explanation: Four squares in a row wrap around the cube as a ring: squares 1 and 3 are opposite, 2 and 4 are opposite, and 1 and 4 meet along an edge.
questions.shortcut: Row of four wraps to a ring.

questions.questionText: A net of six squares has a 2 × 2 block of squares. Can it fold into a cube?
options: Only if the other two squares are separate
No, the squares of the block would overlap
Yes, if the block is at the end
questions.explanation: A cube has only three faces meeting at each corner, but a 2×2 block puts four squares around one point, so the paper would overlap itself and no cube can form.
questions.shortcut: 2×2 block never folds into a cube.
